summary: Many applications secure connections with TLS and X.509 certificates. This document specifies procedures for representing and verifying the identity of application services in those interactions: how a client checks that the certificate matches the server it meant to reach. It obsoletes RFC 6125.

plainLanguage.summary: When a program connects securely to a website, it checks that the certificate the server presents really names the site it asked for. This document sets out exactly which names in a certificate may be used for that check, which may not, and how the comparison is done.

questions: how does tls verify a server certificate name
what is a dns-id in a certificate
can a wildcard certificate match multiple labels
subtitle: How a TLS client decides that the certificate it was given belongs to the service it wanted to reach.

tldr.problem: During a TLS handshake the client has a name in mind, such as the website it asked for, and the server answers with a certificate that carries names of its own. Until the rules for comparing the two are precise, a client can be talked into accepting a certificate for a different service.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines four kinds of identity that can appear in a certificate and says which of them may be checked. The client builds its own list of acceptable identities from the name it was given, then matches that list against the names in the certificate, comparing domain labels case-insensitively and refusing the common name field.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9525 replaces RFC 6125. Wildcard certificates are now the default but the wildcard may only be the whole left-most label, the common name field may no longer be used to identify a service, and IP address identities are added to the list.

today: RFC 9525 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It replaced RFC 6125, which it revises on the basis of a decade of experience, so it is the current specification of how a TLS client verifies a server's identity.

sections.title: Reference Identity and Presented Identity
sections.content:
The visible face of the Internet largely consists of services that use a client-server architecture. When a client communicates with an application service using TLS, DTLS or a protocol built on those, of which QUIC is a notable example, it has some notion of the server's identity, such as the website at bigcompany.example, while attempting to establish secure communication. During TLS negotiation the server presents its notion of the service's identity in the form of a public key certificate issued by a certification authority in the context of the Internet Public Key Infrastructure using X.509.

Informally, the client's idea is the reference identity and the server's is the presented identity. A client needs to verify that the presented identity matches the reference identity so that it can deterministically and automatically authenticate the communication. This document defines the procedures for how clients perform that verification, and therefore defines requirements on other parties, such as the certification authorities that issue certificates, the service administrators requesting them, and the protocol designers defining interactions between clients and servers.

The summary of the rules is short. Only check DNS domain names via the subjectAltName extension designed for that purpose, dNSName. Allow more specific subjectAltName extensions where appropriate, such as uniformResourceIdentifier, iPAddress and the otherName form SRVName. Wildcard support is now the default in certificates, constrained so that the wildcard can only be the complete left-most label of a domain name. Do not include or check strings that look like domain names in the subject's Common Name.
sections.plainLanguage: The client knows which service it wanted, and the server shows a certificate with names on it. The client has to decide whether the certificate really belongs to the service it asked for, and this document defines the test that both sides can rely on.

sections.title: The Four Identifier Types
sections.content:
The document defines four identifier types. DNS-ID is a subjectAltName entry of type dNSName. IP-ID is a subjectAltName entry of type iPAddress. SRV-ID is a subjectAltName entry of type otherName whose name form is SRVName. URI-ID is a subjectAltName entry of type uniformResourceIdentifier.

From the client's point of view some identifiers are direct, because a human user provides them through runtime input, prior configuration or explicit acceptance of a connection attempt. Others are indirect, because the application resolves them automatically from user input, for example a target name resolved from a source name using DNS SRV records. From the service's point of view some identifiers are unrestricted, because they can be used for any type of service, and others are restricted, because they can be used for only one type of service, such as a certificate that can only be used for an IMAP service.

The four types therefore sort as follows. A DNS-ID is direct and unrestricted. An IP-ID is direct and unrestricted. An SRV-ID is typically indirect but can be direct, and it is restricted. A URI-ID is direct and restricted. These distinctions matter because the best practice differs: cross-protocol attacks are possible when two different protocol services use the same certificate, which can be addressed by using restricted identifiers or by deploying services so that they do not share certificates.

The Common Name RDN MUST NOT be used to identify a service because it is not strongly typed, being essentially free-form text, and therefore suffers from ambiguities in interpretation. For similar reasons, other RDNs within the subjectName MUST NOT be used to identify a service.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate can carry four kinds of name. A plain domain name, an IP address, a DNS SRV service name, or a URI. The last two also say which kind of service is being offered, so a certificate that carries one of them can only be used for that service.

sections.title: How a Certificate Should Carry the Identity
sections.content:
When a certification authority issues a certificate based on the FQDN at which the application service provider will provide the application, the rules for representing application service identities apply. The certificate MUST include at least one identifier. It SHOULD include a DNS-ID as a baseline for interoperability, which is not mandatory because it is legitimate for a certificate to include only an SRV-ID or URI-ID so as to scope its use to a particular application type.

If the service deploys a technology whose specification stipulates that certificates should include SRV-IDs, for example XMPP, the certificate SHOULD include an SRV-ID. If the technology stipulates URI-IDs, for example SIP, the certificate SHOULD include a URI-ID whose scheme is that of the protocol and whose host component is the FQDN of the service. The certificate MAY contain more than one DNS-ID, SRV-ID, URI-ID or IP-ID, and MAY include other application-specific identifiers for compatibility with a deployed base.

The document then gives examples. A simple website at www.bigcompany.example, not discoverable via DNS SRV lookups, might have a certificate with only a DNS-ID of www.bigcompany.example. A site reachable at the fixed address 2001:db8::5c might add that value as an IP-ID. An IMAP server at mail.isp.example, discoverable through SRV lookups on isp.example, might carry SRV-IDs of _imap.isp.example and _imaps.isp.example along with DNS-IDs of isp.example and mail.isp.example.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules for what to put in a certificate are short. It needs at least one name, and normally a plain domain name as well so that it works with older clients. A service that has its own kind of identifier should carry that too, so that only that kind of client can use the certificate.

sections.title: How the Client Checks the Identity
sections.content:
At a high level the client verifies the application service's identity by performing three actions. It constructs a list of reference identifiers it would find acceptable, based on the source domain and, if applicable, the type of service it is connecting to. The server provides its presented identifiers in the form of a PKIX certificate. The client then checks each of its reference identifiers against the server's presented identifiers to find a match, matching the source domain of the identifiers and, optionally, their application service type.

The client MUST construct its list of acceptable reference identifiers and MUST do so independently of the identifiers presented by the server. The inputs might be a URI that a user has typed into an interface, configured account information, a hyperlink in a web page, or some other combination that yields a source domain and an application service type.

The rules for building the list are that the reference identifier SHOULD be a URI-ID where the service type is typically associated with a URI for security purposes, and an SRV-ID where the service type is typically discovered by means of DNS SRV records. If the reference identifier is an IP address it is an IP-ID. In the absence of more specific identifiers, the reference identifier is a DNS-ID. Which identifier types the client includes, and their priority, is a matter of local policy.

The client then checks its reference identifiers against the presented identifiers. The search fails if the client exhausts its list without finding a match, and succeeds if any presented identifier matches one of the reference identifiers, at which point the client SHOULD stop the search. A client might also be exposed to identifiers that look like but are not reference identifiers, for example intermediate domain names produced during DNS resolution; unless the application defines a process for authenticating them, those values MUST NOT be treated as reference identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: The client works out on its own what names would be acceptable, without looking at the certificate first, and then compares that list with the names in the certificate. The search stops at the first match, and it fails if none of the acceptable names turns up.

sections.title: The Matching Rules
sections.content:
Each reference identifier produces either a domain name or an IP address and optionally an application service type. A DNS-ID reference identifier must be used directly as the DNS domain name and has no application service type. An IP-ID reference identifier must exactly match the value of an iPAddress entry, with no partial matching, and has no application service type. For an SRV-ID the DNS domain name portion is the Name and the application service type portion is the Service, so an SRV-ID of _imaps.isp.example has a domain name portion of isp.example and a service type of imaps. For a URI-ID the domain name portion is the reg-name part of the host component and the service type is the scheme.

If the domain name portion of a reference identifier is not an internationalized domain name, the matching MUST be performed by comparing the set of domain name labels using a case-insensitive ASCII comparison. If it is an internationalized domain name, the client MUST convert any U-labels to A-labels before checking, and A-labels MUST be compared as case-insensitive ASCII. Each label MUST match in order for the names to be considered a match.

If the technology specification supports wildcards in presented identifiers, the client MUST match the reference identifier against a presented identifier whose domain name portion contains the wildcard character in a label, provided there is only one wildcard character and the wildcard character appears only as the complete content of the left-most label. If the requirements are not met, the presented identifier is invalid and MUST be ignored. A wildcard in a presented identifier can only match one label in a reference identifier, which is not the same as DNS wildcard matching.

Matching of an IP-ID is an octet-for-octet comparison of the bytes of the reference identity with the bytes in the iPAddress entry. For an SRV-ID the application service name MUST be matched case-insensitively, and the underscore is part of the service name. For a URI-ID the scheme name portion MUST be matched case-insensitively.
sections.plainLanguage: The comparison is exact rather than clever. Domain names are compared label by label, ignoring case. A wildcard is only accepted when it is the entire first label, and it stands for exactly one label. IP addresses are compared byte by byte.

sections.title: What to Do When Nothing Matches
sections.content:
If the client has found a presented identifier that matches a reference identifier, the service identity check has succeeded, and the client MUST use the matched reference identifier as the validated identity of the application service.

If no presented identifier matches, the client MUST proceed according to what kind of client it is. An automated application SHOULD terminate the communication attempt with a bad certificate error and log the error appropriately. The application MAY provide a configuration setting to disable this behavior, but it MUST NOT disable this security control by default.

A client directly controlled by a human user SHOULD inform the user of the identity mismatch and automatically terminate the attempt with a bad certificate error, so that users do not inadvertently bypass security protections in hostile situations. Such clients MAY give advanced users the option of proceeding despite the mismatch, but this needs to be handled with extreme caution, for example by first encouraging the user to terminate the attempt and, if they proceed anyway, by forcing them to view the entire certification path.

The application MAY also let the user accept the presented certificate as valid for later connections. Such ad hoc pinning SHOULD NOT restrict future connections to just the pinned certificate, and a local policy that statically enforces a given certificate for a given peer SHOULD be made available as prior configuration rather than as a just-in-time override for a failed connection.
sections.plainLanguage: When nothing matches, the connection is supposed to fail. An automated program should stop and log the error. A program with a person at the keyboard should say what went wrong and stop as well, offering a way to continue only with care.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Wildcard certificates automatically vouch for any single-label hostnames within their domain, but not for multiple levels of domains. That is convenient for administrators but poses the risk of vouching for rogue or buggy hosts. Restricting presented identifiers to only one wildcard character and restricting wildcards to the left-most domain label can help to mitigate certain aspects of the attack described in the referenced paper. Application protocols can also disallow the use of wildcard certificates entirely as a more foolproof mitigation.

For the URI-ID type, the entry MUST include both a scheme and a host component that matches the reg-name rule; if it does not include both it is not a valid URI-ID and MUST be ignored. Any other components are ignored, because only the scheme and host are used for matching.

The TLS Server Name Indication extension only conveys domain names, so a client with an IP-ID reference identity cannot present any information about its reference identity when connecting. Servers that wish to present an IP-ID therefore need to present this identity when a connection is made without SNI.

The specification allows multiple identifiers in one certificate, so a service can use the same certificate for several hostnames or several protocols. The set of names in a certificate is the set of names that could be affected by a compromise of any other server named in the set, so the strength of any server in the set is determined by the weakest of them. The way to mitigate this risk is to limit the number of names any server can speak for and to ensure that all servers in the set have a strong minimum configuration. A client that constructs multiple reference identifiers of different types SHOULD take care to ensure that the issuing certificate authorities are appropriately constrained.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things weaken this check. A wildcard certificate vouches for every host one level down, so a mistake on one machine can look like a mistake on all of them. And a certificate that lists many names means that breaking into any one of those machines can be used to impersonate all the others.
